'''Joseph Caldwell''' (April 21, 1773 &ndash; January 27, 1835) was a [[United States of America|U.S.]] educator, [[Presbyterian]] minister, [[mathematician]], and [[astronomer]].  He was the first president of the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]], holding the office from 1804 until 1812, and from 1816 until his death in 1835.

== Early life and ministry ==
Caldwell was born in [[Lamington, New Jersey]] and graduated from the [[College of New Jersey (18th Century)|College of New Jersey]] (now [[Princeton University|Princeton]]) as Latin salutatorian in 1791.  After graduation he worked as a tutor and was an assistant teacher in [[Elizabeth, New Jersey|Elizabethtown]] before studying for the ministry and obtaining a license to preach from the [[Presbytery of New Brunswick]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Joseph Caldwell Papers, 1791-1835|url=https://finding-aids.lib.unc.edu/00127/|access-date=2021-10-03|website=finding-aids.lib.unc.edu}}</ref>  He was ordained in North Carolina in 1811.<ref>{{Cite web|title=31 May 1811, Page 3 - Weekly Raleigh Register at Newspapers.com|url=http://www.newspapers.com/image/58221343/?terms=Joseph%20Caldwell&match=1|access-date=2021-10-17|website=Newspapers.com|language=en}}</ref>

On October 5, 1822, the North Carolina Synod (Presbyterian) created the Education Society of North Carolina for "the education of indigent and pious youth for the ministry of the gospel", appointing Caldwell as its president.<ref>{{Cite web|title=9 Oct 1822, Page 3 - The Hillsborough Recorder at Newspapers.com|url=http://www.newspapers.com/image/62836240/|access-date=2021-10-17|website=Newspapers.com|language=en}}</ref>

== Educator at the University of North Carolina ==
He became the presiding professor of mathematics at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1797 and later became its president.  After writing the textbook ''A Compendious System of Elementary Geometry (''1822) and other academic works, Caldwell went on to write a series of letters, some under the pen name "Carlton", to advocate for a public education system and for improved transportation in North Carolina.<ref name=":0" />

== Writings as "Carlton" ==
In "The Numbers of Carlton", a set of 22 essays written in 1827-1828, Caldwell presented mathematical analyses to show that a building a central railroad for North Carolina would have economic and accessibility advantages over a system of canals.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Joseph Caldwell, 1773-1835. The Numbers of Carlton, Addressed to the People of North Carolina, on a Central Rail-Road Through the State. The Rights of Freemen is an Open Trade.|url=https://docsouth.unc.edu/nc/caldwell/caldwell.html|access-date=2021-10-26|website=docsouth.unc.edu}}</ref>  These essays, distributed as pamphlets and compiled in book form (in 1828) were influential in winning public support for the railroad.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Numbers of Carlton {{!}} NCpedia|url=https://www.ncpedia.org/numbers-carlton|access-date=2021-10-26|website=www.ncpedia.org}}</ref>  Newspapers like the [[Raleigh Register]] and the [[Hillsborough Recorder]] published them weekly.<ref>{{Cite web|title=1 Oct 1828, Page 2 - The Hillsborough Recorder at Newspapers.com|url=http://www.newspapers.com/image/62836644/?terms=Carlton&match=1|access-date=2021-10-26|website=Newspapers.com|language=en}}</ref>

== Astronomer ==
In 1809, Caldwell was appointed as the "Astronomer" to the commission determining the boundary between North and South Carolina.<ref>{{Cite web|title=13 Apr 1809, Page 3 - Weekly Raleigh Register at Newspapers.com|url=http://www.newspapers.com/image/58222140/?terms=Joseph%20Caldwell&match=1|access-date=2021-10-17|website=Newspapers.com|language=en}}</ref>  When the university declined his request to fund an astronomy program, he purchased telescopes from France with his own money in 1824.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2017-07-24|title=Eyes in the Sky|url=https://college.unc.edu/2017/07/eyes-in-the-sky/|access-date=2021-10-26|website=College of Arts & Sciences|language=en-US}}</ref>  When he constructed the university's astronomical observatory in 1830 in his backyard, it was the first one built solely for educational purposes in the United States.<ref name=":0" />

== Legacy ==
[[File:Joseph Caldwell Monument 4.jpg|thumb|Monument to Joseph Caldwell on UNC campus, with [[Davie Poplar]] in the background]]
In 1841, [[Caldwell County, North Carolina|Caldwell County]] in western North Carolina was named for him.

In October 2013, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill hosted a display to commemorate the role of [[Freemasonry|Masons]] in the establishment of the first public university in the United States. Among items on display were the 18th and 19th-century papers from Eagle Lodge No. 19 in Hillsborough documenting the applications, or “petitions,” of Caldwell to receive the first and second degrees of Masonry.<ref>{{Cite web|last=UNC at Chapel Hill Libraries News and Events|date=October 2, 2013|title=North Carolina's Freemasons and the Cornerstones of UNC|url=http://blogs.lib.unc.edu/news/index.php/2013/10/north-carolinas-freemasons-and-the-cornerstones-of-unc/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/3491/20131123132917/http://blogs.lib.unc.edu/news/index.php/2013/10/north-carolinas-freemasons-and-the-cornerstones-of-unc/|archive-date=November 23, 2013|access-date=}}</ref>
